title: Threats to Internal Validity
description: Master Campbell & Stanley's classic threats: history, maturation, testing, regression to the mean, attrition, and double-blind controls.

slides.title: Campbell & Stanley's Classic Threats 🛡️
slides.content:
# The Enemies of Causal Certainty

**Internal validity** is the degree to which an experiment establishes that the independent variable—and *only* the independent variable—produced the observed changes in the dependent variable. In their landmark work (1966), Donald Campbell and Julian Stanley identified classic threats:

* **History**: Specific external events occurring between pretest and posttest that affect participants (e.g., a national economic crisis occurring during a study on financial anxiety).
* **Maturation**: Natural developmental, physiological, or biological changes occurring within participants over time (e.g., children growing taller, or participants simply getting tired or hungry).
* **Testing Effects**: Taking a pretest changes performance on subsequent posttests due to practice, familiarity, or sensitization.

quizData.question: A researcher measures language skills in 3-year-olds, provides a 12-month educational podcast intervention, and tests them at age 4. Language skills improved significantly. Without a control group, which internal validity threat explains this gain?

options.text: Biological Maturation (normal cognitive brain development occurring between ages 3 and 4)

quizData.explanation: Children naturally undergo massive biological language development between ages 3 and 4; without an untreated control group, gains cannot be attributed to the podcast.

slides.title: Regression to the Mean & Selective Attrition 📉
slides.content:
## More Threats to Watch For

| Threat | Mechanism | Classic Danger Scenario |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Statistical Regression to the Mean** | Extreme scores on an initial test naturally drift closer to the average on re-testing simply due to statistical measurement error | Selecting participants who scored in the bottom 2% of a test; on re-test, their scores will improve even if your intervention is completely useless! |
| **Attrition (Experimental Mortality)** | Participants drop out of the study before completion | If the 15 most depressed patients quit a 12-week drug trial due to side effects, the remaining sample looks artificially healthy! |
| **Instrumentation** | The measuring instrument or human observer changes its calibration over time | Observers becoming more lenient, fatigued, or skilled as the study progresses. |
| **Demand Characteristics** | Cues in the study that reveal the hypothesis to participants | Participants altering answers to please the researcher or confirm expectations. |

A **Double-Blind Placebo-Controlled design**—where neither the participant nor the experimenter knows who receives active treatment—protects against both demand characteristics and experimenter expectancy effects.

slides.title: Internal Validity Check: Regression to the Mean 📊

quizData.question: A clinic selects the 20 patients with the absolute worst depression scores on Monday, gives them a sugar pill on Tuesday, and retests them on Friday. Their average scores improve significantly. What statistical phenomenon is the most likely cause?
quizData.explanation: When individuals are selected based on extreme scores, statistical regression guarantees that random measurement error will average out, moving retest scores toward the mean.

slides.title: Psychology Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
### The True Control Group Cures All

Notice the universal pattern: History, maturation, testing effects, and regression to the mean happen to **both** the treatment group and the control group equally! If your treatment group improves significantly *more* than the control group, you have defeated these threats and proven causality.
